Pandelys Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Panevėžio apskritis, Lithuania

Not demolished. By the late 19th century, Pandelys was almost entirely Jewish — 1,131 of its 1,190 residents in the 1897 census — making it one of the most densely Jewish towns recorded in this collection; the town's own name derives from the Slavic word for Monday, its traditional market day. Pandelys's Jews were strongly Hasidic and Orthodox, influential enough to enforce Sabbath closing hours on local merchants even on the eve of WWII. Following the German occupation of June 1941, the community's exact fate is unclear — some were likely taken to Antanoshe village near Obeliai, documented elsewhere in this collection, and shot alongside Jews from nearby villages, while others may have died in the Velniaduobes forest together with the Jews of Rokiskis. This cemetery, with first burials dating to the mid-18th century, had a water tower built on its grounds during the Soviet era — the same fate as a cemetery in Kupiskis, documented elsewhere in this collection.
